title: Decompressive craniectomy (planned)
subtitle: Large fronto-temporo-parietal craniectomy with expansile duraplasty

indications: Malignant middle cerebral artery infarction: NICE NG128 advises considering decompressive hemicraniectomy, performed within 48 hours of symptom onset, when all its criteria are met (MCA territory deficit with NIHSS above 15, reduced consciousness on NIHSS item 1a, and an infarct of at least half the MCA territory on CT or a large infarct volume on diffusion MRI). NICE removed the previous upper age limit; functional benefit is smaller in older patients.
Traumatic brain injury with intracranial hypertension refractory to tiered medical treatment (secondary decompressive craniectomy), after discussion of the expected outcomes.
Other causes of refractory brain swelling with mass effect, such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or encephalitis, after specialist discussion.
contraindications: A patient or family who, once informed that survival is often with moderate or severe disability, would not want that outcome; the decision rests on values as much as on scans.
Fixed dilated pupils with clinical features of brainstem death or devastating injury where surgery cannot change the outcome.
Uncorrected coagulopathy, including after thrombolysis, until reversed or the timing is agreed.
Severe comorbidity or poor pre-stroke function where the expected outcome is unacceptable to the patient.
preparation: Senior decision with neurocritical care or stroke physicians, documented with the criteria met and the time from onset or from the start of refractory ICP.

Shared decision with the family or the patient's representatives, using decision aids where available. RESCUEicp showed lower mortality but more survivors with vegetative state or severe disability; DECRA showed worse functional outcome after early bifrontal craniectomy for diffuse injury with moderately raised ICP.
Recent CT, coagulation, platelets, cross-match; reversal of antithrombotics.
Plan for the bone flap: local bone bank freezer, or a subcutaneous abdominal pocket.

Consent (or best-interests documentation) should include death, survival with severe disability, haemorrhage (including contralateral haematoma after decompression in trauma), infection, CSF collections and hydrocephalus, seizures, the syndrome of the trephined, and the need for a later cranioplasty with its own risks of infection and bone resorption.
positioning: Supine with a shoulder roll and the head turned to the opposite side, or lateral for a very large decompression.
Horseshoe or pins; the head above the heart, with no jugular compression.
Expose the whole hemicranium from the midline to the ear and from the forehead to behind the parietal eminence, and the abdomen if the flap is to be stored there.
equipment: Craniotomy set: perforator, craniotome, rongeurs (Leksell, Kerrison), bone wax, bipolar diathermy.
Dural substitute or pericranium for an onlay duraplasty.
Sterile containers and labelling for the bone flap, per local bone bank protocol.
anatomy: A reverse question mark (or a T-bar) incision starts in front of the tragus at the zygoma, curves behind the ear and the parietal eminence, and comes forward to the hairline about 2 cm from the midline.
The superficial temporal artery runs in front of the tragus and supplies most of the flap; preserve it.
The frontal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch in the superficial fascia about midway between the tragus and the lateral canthus.
The superior sagittal sinus and its bridging veins lie in the midline; the bone edge is kept about 2 cm lateral to it.
The middle cranial fossa floor and the temporal squama must be removed down to the floor to decompress the temporal lobe off the brainstem.
criticalSafety: Make it large: the Brain Trauma Foundation fourth edition recommends a large fronto-temporo-parietal craniectomy (not less than 12 by 15 cm, or 15 cm diameter) over a small one. A small craniectomy herniates brain through a narrow defect and causes venous infarction at its edge.
Decompress down to the floor of the middle fossa.
Open the dura widely and close it loosely with a graft; never close it tight.
Stay away from the sinus with the bone edge.
In trauma, expect contralateral haematoma when tamponade is released; image early if the brain swells unexpectedly.
structuresAtRisk: Superior sagittal sinus and bridging veins
Superficial temporal artery and the flap blood supply
Frontal branch of the facial nerve
Swollen cortex herniating against the bone edge
commonErrors: A craniectomy that is too small or not taken down to the middle fossa floor.
Bone edge too close to the midline, injuring the sinus.
Incomplete labelling or documentation of the stored bone flap.
Not marking the skin or the notes so that the absence of bone is obvious to the ward team.
complications: Death or survival with severe disability.
New or expanding haematoma, ipsilateral or contralateral.
Wound breakdown or infection, subdural empyema.
Syndrome of the trephined (sinking skin flap), and complications of the later cranioplasty, including infection and bone flap resorption.
postop: Neurocritical care with ICP monitoring if used, and an explicit plan for sedation, blood pressure and osmotherapy targets.
Neurological observations; flap tension recorded. A tense, bulging flap after decompression needs CT.
Protect the unprotected brain: a helmet once mobilising, a note above the bed, and no pressure on the craniectomy side.
Plan the cranioplasty date and bone flap retrieval in the notes and with the family.
Rehabilitation planning and continuing honest prognostic discussion with the family.

steps.emphasis: For many patients this is a best-interests decision with the family; record what outcome they were told to expect.
Record GCS components and pupils; confirm time from stroke onset or the ICP trend that triggered the decision.
State where the bone flap will be stored and that a large craniectomy is planned.
Head turned away with a shoulder roll, high enough to see the zygoma and behind the ear.
Mark the midline, the tragus, the zygoma and a large reverse question mark incision; mark the 2 cm line off the midline.
Include the abdomen if the flap will be stored subcutaneously.
Preserve the superficial temporal artery at the root of the flap.
Large flap: at least 12 by 15 cm, the medial edge about 2 cm from the midline, frontal limit at the floor of the anterior fossa where safe.
A wide stellate or C-shaped opening across the whole defect; open slowly with the anaesthetist ready for a fall in blood pressure.
Unexpected swelling after decompression in trauma suggests a contralateral haematoma: image as soon as the wound is closed.
Expansile onlay duraplasty with pericranium or substitute, laid loosely over the brain. Not watertight, never tight.
Meticulous epidural and bone edge haemostasis; the swollen brain is about to fill the space.
A subgaleal drain on free drainage, not suction, if used.
Close the galea without tension over the swollen brain.
Add flap tension and ICP to the observations, and a sign that there is no bone on that side.
Record the craniectomy dimensions, the dural management, and where and how the bone flap was stored.

step.dc.temporalis.title: Elevating the temporalis muscle
step.dc.temporalis.why: The temporalis covers the temporal squama, which has to be removed to decompress the temporal lobe. Elevating it carefully preserves its blood supply and the frontal branch of the facial nerve, and makes the later cranioplasty easier.
how: Elevate the temporalis with the scalp as a myocutaneous flap, or separately, according to preference and the need for exposure low on the temporal bone.
Divide the muscle close to the superior temporal line, leaving a cuff of fascia for later reattachment if it is elevated separately.
Strip it from the squama subperiosteally down to the zygomatic root and the floor of the middle fossa.
Coagulate the deep temporal arteries as they are met.
structuresAtRisk: Frontal branch of the facial nerve
pitfalls: Leaving the temporalis bulk over the low temporal bone, so the decompression stays high.
Diathermy across the frontal branch at the zygoma.

step.dc.temporal-decompression.title: Decompressing to the floor of the middle fossa
step.dc.temporal-decompression.why: Uncal herniation compresses the brainstem from the temporal lobe. A craniectomy that leaves bone low in the temporal fossa decompresses the convexity but not the brainstem, so the low temporal bone removal is the part of this operation that most changes the outcome.
how: Nibble the remaining temporal squama with rongeurs down to the floor of the middle fossa, flush with the zygomatic root.
Remove the lesser wing of the sphenoid laterally where it narrows the decompression, with wax on the bone edges.
Control the middle meningeal artery with bipolar diathermy as the bone comes off it.
Feel the floor of the middle fossa with a dissector to confirm no ledge remains.
pitfalls: Leaving a temporal ledge that the brain herniates against.
Opening mastoid air cells without waxing them.

step.dc.intradural.title: Intradural inspection and limited evacuation
step.dc.intradural.why: The aim of a decompression is to give the brain room, not to remove brain. Evacuation is limited to clot, and to clearly necrotic contused tissue in trauma; infarcted brain in stroke is left alone.
how: Wash away subdural blood and clot gently with warm irrigation.
Preserve bridging and cortical veins: venous infarction of swollen brain adds to the swelling.
In trauma, remove an acute subdural haematoma and clearly pulped contusion only; do not perform a lobectomy unless that was a planned senior decision.
In malignant infarction, do not resect infarcted brain.
Note the appearance of the brain, its pulsation and whether it lies above or below the bone edge.
structuresAtRisk: Swollen cortex at the bone edge
pitfalls: Resecting viable brain to make closure easier.
Tearing veins while lifting swollen cortex.

step.dc.bone-storage.title: Bone flap storage, labelling and documentation
step.dc.bone-storage.why: The bone flap belongs to the patient and will be returned months later. A lost, unlabelled or contaminated flap commits the patient to a synthetic cranioplasty, and the absence of bone must be obvious to everyone who handles the head.
how: Store the flap by the agreed method: sterile packaging and the hospital bone bank freezer, or a subcutaneous abdominal pocket.
Label it with patient identifiers, the date, the side and the operation, read aloud with the scrub practitioner.
Send a swab for culture if local policy requires it before storage.
Record the storage site, the method and any reference number in the operative note and the bone bank register.
Mark the dressing or the notes to show that there is no bone under the scalp on that side.
pitfalls: Leaving the flap in theatre for 'someone to sort out'.
Not documenting a flap placed in the abdomen.
